segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now a certain man was ill, Lazarus of Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This Mary was the one who anointed the Lord with perfume and wiped his feet with her hair; it was her brother Lazarus who was ill.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the sisters sent word to him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, look, the one you love is ill.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus heard it, he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “This illness is not to end in death, but is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he then stayed two days in the place where he was.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then, after this, he said to the disciples,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Let us go to Judea again.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The disciples said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Rabbi, just now the Judeans were trying to stone you, and you are going back there?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, they do not stumble, because they see the light of this world.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But if anyone walks in the night, they stumble, because the light is not in them.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said these things, and after this he told them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I am going there to wake him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the disciples said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Jesus had spoken about his death, but they thought he was speaking of resting in sleep.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then Jesus told them plainly,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Lazarus has died,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Thomas, who was called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Let us go too, so that we may die with him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus arrived, he found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Bethany was near Jerusalem, about two miles away,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them about their brother.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went to meet him, but Mary stayed sitting in the house.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Martha said to Jesus,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Your brother will rise again.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Martha said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, even if they die, will live,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Yes, Lord. I have come to believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God, the one who is coming into the world.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When she had said this, she went away and called her sister Mary, saying privately,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The Teacher is here and is calling for you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Mary heard this, she got up quickly and went to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Jesus had not yet come into the village but was still at the place where Martha had met him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Jews who were with her in the house, consoling her, saw Mary get up quickly and go out, and they followed her, supposing that she was going to the tomb to weep there.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her weeping, he was stirred with anger in his spirit and deeply troubled,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Where have you laid him?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, come and see.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus wept.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the Jews said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “See how he loved him!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But some of them said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man have done something so that this man too would not die?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus, again stirred with anger within himself, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone lay against it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Take away the stone.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Martha, the sister of the dead man, said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, by now there is a stench, for it has been four days.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Did I not tell you that if you believe you will see the glory of God?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they took away the stone. And Jesus raised his eyes upward and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Father, I thank you that you have heard me.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I knew that you always hear me, but I said this for the sake of the crowd standing around, so that they may believe that you sent me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he had said this, he cried out in a loud voice,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Lazarus, come out!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The dead man came out, his feet and hands bound with strips of cloth and his face wrapped in a cloth. Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Untie him and let him go.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So many of the Jews, those who had come to Mary and seen what he did, believed in him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But some of them went off to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the chief priests and the Pharisees convened a meeting of the council and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What are we doing? For this man is performing many signs.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You know nothing at all,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: nor do you consider that it is to your advantage that one man should die for the people and the whole nation not perish.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He did not say this on his own, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus was going to die for the nation,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the scattered children of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So from that day on they planned to kill him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Jesus no longer walked about openly among the Jews, but went away from there to the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and there he stayed with the disciples.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the Passover of the Jews was near, and many went up to Jerusalem from the countryside before the Passover to purify themselves.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they were looking for Jesus and saying to one another as they stood in the temple,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What do you think? Surely he will not come to the festival?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that anyone who knew where he was should report it, so that they might arrest him.

notes.phrase: the one who anointed the Lord with perfume
notes.note: The anointing is not narrated until the next chapter (12:1–8). The narrator identifies Mary by it here, which suggests the story was already well known to the first readers.

The Greek word can mean both “Jews” and “Judeans.” Here the point is geographic: Jesus has just proposed returning to Judea, and the disciples, themselves Jews, object that people there had tried to stone him. Elsewhere in the chapter the word is rendered “Jews.” Scholars are divided on how far “Judeans” should be used in John.

The verb is the ordinary Greek word for “save,” used for rescue and healing as well as for salvation. The disciples mean only that sleep is a good sign in a sick man. A reader of John may also hear the fuller sense “he will be saved.”
The Greek says “about fifteen stadia.” A stadion was roughly 185 meters (about 600 feet), so the distance is a little under two miles, or about three kilometers.

The Greek word means “anointed one” and translates the Hebrew title “Messiah,” the king Israel expected. Martha is confessing a title, not using a name, so “Messiah” is used here, as in several modern translations. “Christ” is kept where the word functions as a name.

notes.phrase: was stirred with anger in his spirit
notes.traditional: was deeply moved in spirit (KJV: groaned in the spirit)
notes.note: Outside this chapter the verb is used of stern warning or indignant scolding (Mark 1:43; 14:5), and in wider Greek of angry snorting. It does not elsewhere mean grief or tenderness. Most English versions soften it to “deeply moved,” but many commentators hold that anger or indignation is meant, whether at death itself or at the unbelief around him; the text does not say which. The same verb recurs in verse 38.

The verb is not the one used for Mary and the mourners in verses 31 and 33, which often implies loud lament. This one, found only here in the New Testament, means to shed tears. Many take its tense to mean “burst into tears.”

notes.traditional: he hath been dead four days
notes.note: Burial normally took place on the day of death. Later rabbinic tradition records a belief that the soul lingered near the body for three days. It is uncertain whether this belief was current in Jesus’s time, but the fourth day in any case puts the death beyond all doubt.

“Place” most likely means the temple, which was commonly called “the place” or “the holy place.” It could also mean Jerusalem, or the council’s own position and standing. The literal word is kept so that the reader can weigh these.

The Greek word is the one translated “Gentiles” elsewhere when it is plural and refers to the non-Jewish peoples. In the singular it means a people as a national unit, here the Jewish nation. In verse 50 Caiaphas sets it beside a different word, “people,” the usual scriptural term for Israel as God’s people.

notes.traditional: the high priest that same year
notes.note: The high priesthood was not an annual office; Caiaphas held it for nearly two decades, from about AD 18 to 36. “That year” most likely means “in that fateful year,” the year of Jesus’s death. The same Greek word in the plural is rendered “chief priests,” meaning the leading priestly families.

candidates.reason: Versions split between “deeply moved” in John 11 and “sternly warn/scold” in Mark and Matthew; one decision on whether the anger sense is carried through is needed.
The sleep-for-death euphemism recurs in Matthew, Acts, 1 Corinthians and 1 Thessalonians, and translations vary between “fall asleep” and “die.”
Distances in the Gospels and the symbolic figures in Revelation need one policy: convert to modern units or keep “stadia.”
It recurs across the Gospels and Acts, and translators vary between “Sanhedrin,” “council” and “the Council.”
One Greek word gets two English renderings by number; the split should be fixed and explained uniformly across the Gospels, Acts and Hebrews.
